item.title: The climate finance paradox. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Climate finance has become one of the central topics in the global climate change discourse. Every Conference of Parties (COP) under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) discusses billions of dollars in climate finance and announces new commitments, making pledges and debating on how financial resources should be mobilized.
From COP15 in Copenhagen to COP30 in Brazil, the concept of climate finance has evolved significantly, reshaping both global negotiations and expectations.
The Copenhagen Accord marked a turning point by making a commitment to mobilize $100 billion annually and paving the way for the establishment of the Green Climate Fund (GCF). The Paris Agreement adopted at COP21 in 2015 further institutionalized the climate finance architecture, placing it at the centre of global efforts to support mitigation, adaptation and resilience-building in developing countries. More recently, COP29, widely described as the “finance COP,” adopted New Quantified Climate Goals (NCQG) and agreed to mobilize $300bn per year by 2035.
Yet the outcome also exposed a widening gap between ambition and reality. While developing and least developed countries argued that around $5-6 trillion was required annually to meet the global climate goals, the negotiated amount stood at only $300bn. How these resources will be mobilized, delivered, and accessed remains unresolved.
An uncomfortable question also remains: Has climate finance actually strengthened the resilience of countries like Bangladesh?
The answer is not as straightforward as the volume of funding might suggest.
Much of the climate finance debate continues to focus on how much money is committed or disbursed. Success is often measured in mobilization of millions or billions of dollars, the number of approved projects, or the volume of international funding received.
While these figures are important, they reveal very little about whether climate finance is creating long-term resilience where it matters most.
Although the Paris agreement didn’t mention the word “compensation,” for developed nations, climate finance is considered an obligation arising from historical responsibility for greenhouse gas emissions.
For developing and least developed countries, it is a matter of climate justice, recognizing that those who have contributed the least to climate change are experiencing the worst consequences of climate change.
Even when finance becomes available, accessing funds is rarely straightforward. Climate finance operates through an increasingly complex architecture involving multilateral funds, bilateral agencies, development banks, accreditation processes, fiduciary standards, environmental safeguards, and reporting requirements.
While these mechanisms are designed to ensure accountability and effectiveness, they also increase transaction costs and create significant barriers, particularly for countries with limited institutional capacity.
Climate finance therefore does not move directly from international commitments to the vulnerable communities. It passes through a complex pathway of institutions, governance systems, and political processes before reaching those most vulnerable to climate change.
The gap between the demand and announced amount is not the only problem in the climate finance discussion. Accessing climate finance for the least developed and developing countries is also a challenge for both the capacity gap and the complex mechanism of the climate finance instruments.
The Paris Agreement encourages countries to pursue low-carbon and climate-resilient development. However, for many developing countries, climate action cannot be separated from broader development priorities.
Governments must simultaneously reduce poverty, create employment, expand infrastructure, strengthen health and education systems, and improve food security. A ccessing funds remains a major challenge for many countries like Bangladesh which are the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries.
Bangladesh has emerged as one of the more pro-active countries in strengthening climate governance. Over the past decade, Bangladesh has established an impressive policy architecture, including the Bangladesh Climate Change Strategy and Action Plan, the National Adaptation Plan, a nd the Delta Plan 2100. Climate considerations are increasingly integrated into national planning and budgeting systems, while institutions responsible for climate governance have continued to evolve.
However, Bangladesh continues to seek enormous investment requirements for climate adaptation, resilient infrastructure, disaster risk reduction, renewable energy, urban development, and climate-induced displacement. These investments are essential not only for responding to climate change but also for boosting economic growth and improving living standards.
The challenge is therefore much broader than accessing climate finance. Bangladesh is expected to achieve low-carbon development while continuing its journey towards upper-middle-income status.
It must invest in clean energy while ensuring affordable electricity for industries and households. It must strengthen climate resilience while expanding infrastructure. It must reduce emissions while creating employment for a growing population. It must support climate adaptation while financing education, healthcare, social protection. and urban services.
In other words, Bangladesh is expected to pursue climate resilience and economic prosperity simultaneously.
The difficulty lies in the fact that the current climate finance architecture has not yet evolved to adequately support this bi-fold ambition.
Low carbon and climate-resilient development cannot be purchased simply by increasing financial commitments. It requires institutional readiness, coherent public policy, strong local governments, effective planning and budgeting systems, private sector engagement, and long-term investment strategies.
Finance remains indispensable, but finance alone cannot transform development pathways.
Developing countries cannot afford to pursue climate objectives at the expense of economic development. Nor can they postpone climate action until prosperity has been achieved. The challenge is to integrate both objectives within a balanced development strategy.
This requires moving beyond a project-based approach towards financing structural transformation.
Climate finance should strengthen national planning systems rather than creating parallel implementation structures. It should empower local governments alongside national institutions. It should mobili z e private investment without undermining public accountability.
Above all, it should recogni z e that development and climate action are mutually reinforcing rather than competing objectives.
An equally important question deserves greater attention: W hat kind of financial architecture enables developing countries to simultaneously achieve prosperity, resilience, and low-carbon development?
Greater financial commitments remain essential. Vulnerable countries have repeatedly argued that existing available resources are limited compared to actual requirements. However, increasing the volume of finance alone will not resolve the underlying paradox.
The international community must also make climate finance more predictable, accessible, and aligned with national development priorities of the countries who are experiencing challenges of balancing economic prosperity and achieving climate goals.
Funding mechanisms should reduce unnecessary complexity while strengthening country ownership. Institutional readiness should be rewarded through more flexible access to finance rather than additional procedural burdens.
Most importantly, global climate finance should recogni z e that successful climate action in developing countries depends not only on reducing emissions but also on creating the economic opportunities that allow societies to thrive.
The c limate f inance p aradox reminds us that expanding ambitions require equally ambitious financial and institutional reforms. Without closing the gap between expectations and implementation, developing countries will continue to face an impossible task: D elivering prosperity on a low-carbon development pathway with financial support that remains insufficient, fragmented, and difficult to access.
Bangladesh’s experience shows that the challenge is not a lack of commitment. The challenge is ensuring that the global climate finance architecture evolves as rapidly as the ambitions it now seeks to achieve.
Md Abul Basar is an anthropologist and governance expert, and serves as the team lea der at a Switzerland-based international organization. He can be reached at bashar.arif@gmail.com .

item.title: Treating e-waste as an opportunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
That Bangladesh generates an estimated three million metric tons of electronic waste annually, and that it recycles less than 10% of that waste through formal channels, is an extremely concerning reality for a nation that has aspirations of a more sustainable future.
That the majority of our e-waste ends up in informal scrapyards, landfills, and waterways, where toxic materials contaminate the soil and air, stand in sharp contradiction to our desire for a healthier country. It is safe to say that such negligence is no longer just an environmental concern but a public health and governance crisis.
The prevalence of informal recyclers dominating the sector, often working without protective gear while handling lead, mercury, cadmium, and other hazardous substances, also reflects poorly on the present state of affairs. Workers who are often below the age of 18 are frequently exposed to these toxins, with long‑term consequences for cognitive and physical development.
The other component to this failure is that Bangladesh is also losing economic value. E‑waste contains recoverable materials - copper, gold, and other rare earth elements - that could support a circular economy and create jobs, with reports stating that Bangladesh could recover over $200 million in resources annually through effective recycling.
Instead, these resources are being discarded or extracted unsafely, with no national system to capture their value.
The solution is clear, and it starts with recognizing recycling firstly as a moral imperative but also as a means to generate value. This means investing to build a nationwide collection network and modern recycling facilities while formalizing the informal sector with training and safety standards.
E‑waste is not garbage but an opportunity. Managed well, it can reduce pollution, recover valuable materials, and support our sustainable growth. Managed poorly, it will continue to be one of our most dangerous pollutants. The choice is clear.

item.title: Heat resilience must be a national priority. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The World Bank’s latest findings should alarm every policy-maker in Bangladesh: As per the the report, “A Livable Future: Protecting Jobs and Growth from Extreme Heat in South Asia's Cities,” extreme heat cost our nation $18 billion in lost labour productivity and wiped out 465,000 jobs in Dhaka alone in 2024.
That this is projected to double in about 50 years is a reality we must prepare for from today itself, and do all we can to ensure that the worst does not come to pass.
What is most distressing about this is that it is hitting the poorest workers the hardest, thereby contributing to our widening inequality and undermining our development trajectory.
Our cities, especially Dhaka, have been trapped in a dangerous cycle of rising temperatures, expanding concrete, shrinking green spaces, and worsening air quality. The result has been all too predictable, with workers unable to continue or facing unbearable conditions to continue working.
To say Bangladesh must build heat‑resilient towns and cities is a gross understatement at this point. It is something we should have been planning for decades earlier.
However, given the exponential damage extreme heat does to our nation on a yearly basis, it is time to begin redesigning urban spaces with shade, ventilation, and greenery, enforcing building codes that reduce heat absorption, expanding our tree cover in our cities, and enact major reforms such as rethinking our transport infrastructure.
Better, more sustainable urban development is no longer optional but a survival strategy. Continuing to expand as a heat trap is not a solution, nor can it be classified as development. We must shift toward climate‑sensitive planning that prioritizes human health and economic resilience.
Extreme heat is already costing billions and destroying livelihoods. Without urgent action, the losses will continue to grow. We must treat heat resilience as a national priority. Our future depends on it.

item.title: Poison on our plates. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Food safety and environmental protection are inseparable pillars of sustainable development. A nation cannot claim genuine progress while its citizens are exposed to contaminated food and its natural environment continues to deteriorate.
Unfortunately, Bangladesh faces serious challenges in both areas, demanding stronger governance, institutional accountability, and unwavering political commitment.
Reports concerning food contamination have raised widespread public concern. Laboratory findings reportedly conducted by Professor Dr Abul Hossain of the Department of Chemistry, University of Dhaka, indicated elevated levels of chromium in broiler chicken meat, liver, brain, and commercial eggs. These findings have been attributed to the alleged use of chromium-contaminated tannery waste in poultry and fish feed, despite reported judicial restrictions on such practices.
Concerns have also been expressed regarding arsenic and other hazardous substances in farmed fish. If confirmed through independent scientific investigation, such contamination poses a serious threat to public health and demands immediate regulatory action.
When I joined the Bangladesh civil service, food adulteration was comparatively rare. Consumers generally had greater confidence in the quality of food, and ethical business practices were more widely respected.
Today, however, food adulteration has become a significant public health concern. Yet this problem is neither inevitable nor impossible to solve. It requires honest leadership, effective law enforcement, public awareness, and accountability at every level.
During my tenure as a Deputy Commissioner, I personally led campaigns against food adulteration, particularly during Ramadan, when the use of unauthorized colours and harmful chemical additives in iftar items was frequently reported. Regular mobile courts, market inspections, and coordinated enforcement by executive magistrates and law enforcement agencies significantly improved compliance.
Although some business leaders initially questioned these measures, I asked one of them a simple question: “Would you like your own children to consume adulterated food?” His answer was an immediate “No.”
That response reflected a universal truth -- every parent wants safe food for their family. Protecting public health should therefore unite, rather than divide, regulators and the business community.
Bangladesh also needs stronger environmental governance. Over the years, substantial public resources and international assistance have been invested in forestry, biodiversity conservation, and climate adaptation projects. While many initiatives have contributed positively, questions have also been raised regarding the effectiveness and transparency of certain projects.
Public investment should always be measured by tangible environmental outcomes -- such as increased forest cover, biodiversity conservation, pollution reduction, and climate resilience -- rather than by expenditure alone. Whenever credible allegations of irregularities arise, they should be investigated independently and impartially to strengthen public confidence.
The same principle applies to institutions responsible for environmental regulation and food safety. Their success should be judged by measurable improvements in environmental quality and consumer protection, not merely by administrative reports or completed projects. Strong institutions require transparency, professional competence, and accountability.
Although Bangladesh has enacted important legislation, including the Safe Food Act 2013, effective implementation remains the greatest challenge to its success.
Regulatory agencies must strengthen laboratory testing, surveillance, market inspections, and enforcement across the entire food supply chain. Equally important, officials who fail to discharge their statutory responsibilities through negligence or wilful inaction should, where legally appropriate, be held accountable.
Environmental crimes and deliberate food adulteration should not be treated as ordinary regulatory violations. They threaten human health, damage biodiversity, increase healthcare costs, and undermine sustainable development.
Consideration should therefore be given to strengthening penalties for serious offences, ensuring swift prosecution, and enhancing judicial capacity to deal with crimes that endanger public health and the environment.
Public awareness is equally essential. Governments, educational institutions, businesses, civil society, religious leaders, and the media all have a shared responsibility to promote a culture that values environmental stewardship and rejects food adulteration.
Sustainable progress cannot be achieved through laws alone; it depends on ethics, integrity, and collective responsibility.
Bangladesh has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to overcome major national challenges. There is every reason to believe that the country can also become a regional leader in food safety and environmental protection.
Achieving this goal, however, requires a genuine policy of zero tolerance toward food adulteration and environmental crimes, supported by strong institutions, transparent governance, scientific evidence, and the consistent application of the rule of law.
Protecting the environment and ensuring safe food are not merely administrative obligations -- they are moral responsibilities owed to every citizen.
Mizanul Hoque Chowdhury is a former Additional Secretary, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Bangladesh.

item.title: Pakistan pitches textiles amid new US tariffs. [ dawn ]
item.description:
NEW YORK: Pakistan is using one of North America’s largest textile sourcing exhibitions to strengthen its position in the US market as exporters confront new American tariffs and rising production costs amid growing regional competition.

The Pakistan Pavilion at Texworld New York City 2026 opened on Wednesday at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Centre, where five manufacturers are showcasing home textiles, apparel, leather garments, sportswear, gloves and other value-added products for buyers from across the US and overseas.

Organised by the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan (TDAP) in collaboration with the Trade and Investment Wing of Pakistan’s Consulate General in New York, the pavilion showcases A1 Infinity, MRI Group, Hometex Corporation, Ruqi Sports and Niza Sports.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, Pakistan’s Ambassador to the US, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh, described the textile sector as “the backbone of Pakistan’s export economy” and reaffirmed the government’s commitment to expanding exports and to strengthening commercial ties with the US.

10pc duty could cost exporters $2 billion

Textiles and apparel account for the overwhelming majority of Pakis­tan’s exports to the US, while the remainder includes rice, leather products, surgical instruments, sports goods and other manufactured items. Ready-made garments, knitwear and home textiles remain the country’s leading export categories.

Pakistan’s participation comes less than a week after the Office of the US Trade Represen­tative imposed a new 10pc ad valorem tariff on Pakistani imports under Section 301, effective July 24.

The measure followed a US investigation into enforcement of forced-labour import prohibitions in 60 trading partners. While acknowledging that Pakistan legally prohibits forced labour, the USTR said enforcement needed to be streng­­thened, placing the country among those subject to the additional duty.

The tariff follows months of uncertainty over US trade policy. Earlier this year, Wash­ing­ton proposed reciprocal tariffs of up to 29pc on Pakistani goods before negotiations reportedly lowered the baseline rate. Exporters fear that the latest duties, combined with rising domestic production costs, could erode Pakistan’s competitiveness in its most important export market.

Analysts estimate the new tariff could reduce Pakistan’s textile exports by about $564m in FY26, with losses potentially exceeding $2 billion if American buyers shift sourcing to lower-cost suppliers.

Pakistan already faces strong competition from Bangladesh, India, Vietnam and China while domestic manufacturers continue to contend with high energy prices, expensive financing, rising taxes and logistics costs.

item.title: Saving our tigers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The revelation that Bangladesh has only 189 tigers left should be treated for what it is - a national tragedy.
The Royal Bengal Tiger is the most iconic species we have as a nation, it is quite literally the symbol of our natural heritage. That its numbers keep dwindling, and State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin warning that the current situation is not sufficient to protect the species from extinction, is deeply concerning.
When tiger numbers continue to fall, it signals deeper ecological distress that cannot be ignored. Experts have long cautioned that habitat loss, rising salinity, human encroachment, poaching, and climate‑driven changes in the Sundarbans are eroding the conditions tigers need to survive. The latest numbers only confirm that these pressures are intensifying.
Conserving tigers should not be viewed as only about protecting a single species. It is about safeguarding the entire biodiversity of the Sundarbans - our most critical natural buffer against natural disasters such as cyclones and tidal surges.
Bangladesh has taken steps: Strengthening patrols, expanding camera‑trap monitoring, and improving community engagement. However, it is plain to see that the scale of the challenge demands more.
Conservation must be backed by sustained investment, scientific research, and strict enforcement against poaching and illegal resource extraction. The forest also needs better protection from industrial pressures, unregulated tourism, and climate impacts that are already reshaping its landscape.
We must also broaden our focus beyond tigers. Biodiversity loss has been accelerating nationwide, from wetlands to hill forests to coastal ecosystems. Protecting wildlife therefore requires a holistic strategy, from restoring habitats to regulating development to integrating conservation into national planning rather than treating it as an isolated sector.
The tiger population can recover, but only if we are able to act decisively, consistently, and with long‑term vision. Saving the tiger means saving the Sundarbans, and saving the Sundarbans means protecting our future.

item.title: Winning the fight against trafficking. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Today is World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, and is a reminder that human trafficking remains one of the most persistent and damaging crimes. Every year, thousands of Bangladeshis fall victim to traffickers.
Yet, trafficking is no longer confined to borders, brokers, or physical coercion. Much of it has moved online, and we are now facing a new generation of threats that exploit digital technology, social media, and the vulnerabilities of young people seeking opportunity.
Human trafficking has always preyed on desperation. Today, it also preys on connectivity. Recruiters no longer need to visit villages or operate through local agents; they can reach victims through Facebook groups, messaging apps, job portals, and livestream platforms.
From false job offers to fraudulent migration schemes, the digital shift has made trafficking faster, harder to detect, and easier to disguise as legitimate opportunity.
For Bangladesh, this evolution is especially dangerous. Millions of young people are online, often without digital literacy or awareness of the risks. Migrant workers increasingly rely on social media for job information. Traffickers have adapted, and our protection systems must adapt with equal speed.
Bangladesh has made progress in combating traditional trafficking routes, strengthening laws, and improving rescue and rehabilitation. But the digital dimension remains under-addressed.
Law enforcement lacks specialized cyber‑trafficking units. Border and migration officials are not always trained to identify victims recruited online. And survivors often struggle to navigate the legal system when exploitation begins on a screen rather than at a border.
On this day, the message is clear: Strengthening protection means also strengthening digital vigilance. Traffickers are online and Bangladesh must be ready to meet them there. Trafficking has changed and our response must change with it. We cannot rely on old tools to fight a new threat.

item.title: When childhood becomes the first casualty of climate change. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There was a time when climate change in Bangladesh was discussed through the language of infrastructure. The conversation revolved around embankments, cyclone shelters, flood control projects, adaptation funds, and carbon emissions. Success was measured by the number of kilometres of embankments built or the amount of international climate finance secured. Children appeared in these discussions only as passive victims to be rescued after disaster struck.
The latest Children’s Climate Risk Report 2026 by Unicef demands that we abandon that habit of thinking. It suggests something far more unsettling. Bangladesh is not merely fighting a climate crisis. It is slowly becoming a place where childhood itself is being reshaped by an environment that is growing increasingly hostile.
This is perhaps the most important lesson hidden beneath the report’s alarming statistics. Climate change is no longer only about damaged roads, submerged villages or destroyed crops. It is altering what it means to grow up in Bangladesh.
The report places Bangladesh fourth among the countries where children face the highest climate risks, with an overall vulnerability score of 9.38 out of 10. Only Myanmar, Pakistan, and Vietnam rank higher. Bangladesh receives the maximum possible risk score, 10 out of 10, for riverine flooding, making its children the most exposed in the world to this particular hazard. The country’s scores remain alarmingly high across nearly every category, including tropical cyclones at 9.7, air pollution at 9.7, drought at 9.65, extreme heat at 9.24, and coastal flooding at 8.13.
These numbers are disturbing enough. Yet the real story lies in what they collectively reveal.
Climate disasters rarely arrive one at a time anymore. Bangladesh increasingly experiences overlapping emergencies where one hazard begins before another has fully disappeared. Floods are followed by disease outbreaks. Cyclones are followed by prolonged displacement. Heatwaves arrive before communities recover from previous disasters. Air pollution quietly intensifies throughout the year, affecting children even when skies appear clear.
The report captures this reality by arguing that Bangladeshi children are exposed not to isolated disasters but to multiple climate shocks simultaneously.
Nearly 60 million children in Bangladesh are exposed to at least one climate-related hazard. More than 24 million face the combined risks of floods, droughts, and cyclones. Around 32 million children are directly threatened by riverine flooding, about 22 million by cyclones, while roughly 60 million are exposed to drought and air pollution.
These figures are difficult to comprehend because they describe an entire generation rather than isolated communities.
The tendency is often to think of climate change through dramatic images of flooded villages or collapsing riverbanks. Those images matter, but they obscure a slower crisis unfolding inside classrooms, hospitals, and homes.
When schools become shelters after cyclones, education stops. When repeated flooding destroys family income, children become workers instead of students. When prolonged displacement breaks community networks, girls become more vulnerable to early marriage while boys face greater pressure to enter informal labour markets. Health deteriorates because clean drinking water becomes scarce, sanitation systems collapse and disease spreads more easily.
The damage extends well beyond the immediate disaster.
A child who misses several months of education today may experience lower earnings decades later. A malnourished infant exposed to repeated climate shocks may never fully recover physically or cognitively. Psychological trauma caused by repeated disasters often remains invisible, although it shapes behaviour and emotional well-being for years.
These are losses that no disaster compensation package can fully repair.
One of the most overlooked findings in the Unicef report is that Bangladesh actually performs comparatively better in several traditional child development indicators such as child health, nutrition, education, poverty reduction, and maternal mortality. In other words, the country has made genuine progress over the past decades.
Yet climate change threatens to reverse those achievements. The environmental conditions necessary to sustain these gains are becoming increasingly unstable. Development successes built over decades now stand on uncertain ecological foundations.
Perhaps this explains why conventional adaptation strategies increasingly appear insufficient.
Much of Bangladesh’s climate planning understandably focuses on physical infrastructure. Cyclone shelters save lives. Embankments reduce flood damage. River dredging improves water management. These remain essential investments.
However, the next stage of adaptation requires a different question. Instead of asking how infrastructure survives climate change, policy-makers must ask how childhood survives climate change.
These are not identical questions. Children experience disasters differently from adults because their bodies, minds, and futures are still developing. A week without school affects an eight-year-old differently than it affects a thirty-year-old office worker. Air pollution permanently damages developing lungs more severely than adult lungs. Malnutrition during childhood produces lifelong consequences that cannot simply be reversed later.
The report estimates that around 337 million children worldwide face riverine flooding, 662 million face tropical storms, 33 million are exposed to coastal flooding, approximately 1.2 billion experience extreme heat and nearly 1.8 billion face drought. Around 80% of children exposed to riverine and coastal flooding live in only 10 countries, with Bangladesh among the most heavily affected.
These global figures remind us that Bangladesh occupies the frontline of a worldwide crisis. Yet unlike wealthier nations, Bangladesh must confront this emergency while still addressing poverty, rapid urbanization, infrastructure deficits, and demographic pressures.
This makes policy choices especially important. Climate adaptation cannot remain concentrated only within environment ministries. It must become the organizing principle across education, public health, urban planning, and social protection.
A single national blueprint cannot adequately protect them all. Floating schools may be appropriate in flood-prone wetlands. Residential educational facilities may prove more effective in remote hill regions. Coastal districts require stronger shelter systems designed specifically around children’s needs. Urban schools increasingly need shaded environments capable of protecting students during prolonged heatwaves.
Climate adaptation succeeds only when geography shapes policy. Equally important is recognizing that children are not merely recipients of protection.
Young people increasingly understand climate risks because they experience them firsthand. Many already participate in community preparedness programs, environmental campaigns, and local adaptation initiatives. Their perspectives often reveal practical problems adults overlook.
Treating children solely as vulnerable populations ignores their potential as active participants in building resilience.
Unicef rightly argues that children should be meaningfully included in climate policy-making. This is not symbolic participation. It reflects the reality that today’s policy decisions will define their entire futures far more than they will affect current decision-makers.
There is also an uncomfortable issue the international community cannot continue avoiding. Bangladeshi children contribute almost nothing to global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet they bear some of the world’s highest climate risks.
This remains one of the greatest moral failures of modern international politics. The countries and populations least responsible for warming the planet continue paying its highest human costs. Climate justice therefore cannot remain confined to abstract diplomatic language during international summits. It must translate into predictable adaptation finance, technology transfer, and long-term investments focused specifically on children’s well-being.
HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Trapped behind the scam. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In November last year, a young man named Abdullah Molla left Bangladesh for Cambodia, believing he had found a proper office job. What he found instead was captivity. He was pushed into an online scam compound, stripped of his documents, and held until his family, back home, borrowed heavily to buy his freedom.
Another Bangladeshi, Shafiqul Islam Hridoy, was promised $800 a month for data entry work. He was locked in a dark room for 17 days, beaten, and given electric shocks, because he refused to defraud strangers online.
According to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, more than 300 Bangladeshis have already been rescued and repatriated from scam compounds in Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam, and elsewhere in Southeast Asia.
These are not distant tragedies. They are warnings written for Bangladesh, and we should read them carefully.
This year, the United Nations has chosen "Trapped Behind the Scam" as the theme for the World Day Against Trafficking in Persons. It is a deliberate shift in language.
For decades, the world pictured trafficking as physical movement into brothels, farms, or households. Today's traffickers have found a subtler and more profitable model: They recruit a person with a fake job advertisement, fly them across a border, take their passport, and force them to sit at a computer scamming other people, often for 18 hours a day, under threats of violence.
The United Nations Human Rights Office recently estimated that at least 300,000 people are held inside these scam compounds across the Mekong region alone, generating an estimated $64bn a year for organized crime. Interpol has confirmed that victims now come from at least 66 countries. Bangladesh is one of them.
Why this should worry us
It is tempting to treat this as someone else's crisis, a problem for Cambodia or Myanmar to solve. That comfort is misplaced. Bangladesh carries exactly the vulnerabilities that this new form of trafficking is built to exploit.
Consider the numbers. The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics counted 1.94 million unemployed young people in its last full Labour Force Survey, and nearly a third of them held a university degree. An educated, underemployed, internet-literate youth population is not a liability by itself. But it is precisely the profile that scam recruiters look for, because fluent, tech-comfortable workers make more convincing scammers.
The same digital reach that lets a Dhaka graduate apply for a freelance job in London also lets a trafficker in Phnom Penh place a fraudulent advertisement on her Facebook feed. Add to this a well-worn migration culture, hundreds of thousands of Bangladeshis travel abroad for work every year, often through informal sub-agents rather than licensed recruiters, and the pathway from a hopeful jobseeker to a captive scammer becomes disturbingly short.
The US State Department's most recent Trafficking in Persons report on Bangladesh makes a further point worth sitting with: Traffickers are now using social media, mobile messaging, and artificial intelligence to identify and lure victims, particularly women and girls, with the same fluency that legitimate recruiters use to fill real vacancies. The tools of opportunity and the tools of exploitation have become almost indistinguishable.
A pattern Bangladesh already knows
None of this is entirely new to us. Bangladesh has long struggled with labour trafficking, child marriage-linked exploitation, domestic servitude, and cross-border trafficking involving the Rohingya population.
What online scam trafficking adds is a digital front door to an old house. The victim no longer needs to be poor, illiterate, or desperate in the ways we once assumed. She may have a smartphone, a degree, and a LinkedIn profile. That should unsettle our awareness campaigns, most of which still picture trafficking as something that happens to people with few choices, not people who believed they were making a smart one.
What Bangladesh has already done, and what is still missing
There is real progress to acknowledge. In a significant and timely step, Bangladesh has this year replaced its 2012 anti-trafficking law with the Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Prevention and Suppression Act, 2026.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has described it as designed specifically to address crimes carried out through digital platforms and technology, a direct acknowledgement that our legal framework had fallen behind the criminals it was meant to stop.
The new law separates trafficking from migrant smuggling for the first time, strengthens investigation powers, allows the freezing of trafficking-linked assets, and enshrines the principle that a rescued victim should not be prosecuted as a criminal.
Alongside it, the judiciary has received a new Bench Book, developed with UNODC and the European Union, to help judges handle trafficking cases with the trauma-informed sensitivity these cases demand.
These are meaningful reforms. But laws only work when they are enforced, and enforcement in this space is unusually hard. Investigators need the capacity to trace cryptocurrency payments and follow evidence across borders. Diplomatic missions need faster channels to identify and repatriate victims held in remote compounds.
And crucially, our law enforcement and immigration officers need to be trained to recognize a rescued scam-centre worker as a trafficking victim first, not a cybercriminal. Abdullah Molla and Shafiqul Islam Hridoy were fortunate to come home. Many others, still trapped or too ashamed and indebted to seek help, are not.
A way forward
Protecting Bangladeshis from this crime does not require reinventing the wheel; it requires connecting pieces we already have.
Recruitment agencies and job platforms should be required to verify overseas postings before they are advertised. Bangladesh Bank and the Anti-Corruption Commission should be brought more closely into trafficking investigations, since this crime moves through financial systems as much as through borders.
Our missions abroad, particularly in Southeast Asia, need standing protocols for identifying and repatriating trafficking victims quickly. And our schools, universities, and job-training centres should teach a simple, urgent lesson: A job offer that asks you to hand over your passport, or that came from someone you have only ever met on Telegram, deserves suspicion before it deserves an air ticket.
Human trafficking no longer waits at the border. It arrives as a notification on a phone. If Bangladesh wants to protect the very opportunities that digital life offers our young people, our vigilance has to move online too, before more of our sons and daughters mistake a scam compound for a career.
Inmanuel Chayan Biswas, a humanitarian and development practitioner, is working for a prominent NGO in Bangladesh.

item.title: Litton Das replaces Mehidy Hasan as Bangladesh ODI captain. [ dawn ]
item.description:
DHAKA: Wicket-keeper/batter Litton Das has replaced Mehidy Hasan Miraz as captain of Bangladesh’s One-day International team, the country’s cricket board said on Wednesday.

Mehidy’s captaincy exit comes after Bangladesh ODI series defeat against Zimbabwe earlier this month. Najmul Hossain will continue in his role as Test captain.

The appointment of Litton, who is already the T20 skipper, as the white-ball leader comes as Bangladesh’s move to split captaincy ahead of next year’s ODI World Cup in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe.

“I and the board believe we should have two captains — a white-ball and a red-ball captain,” Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) president Tamim Iqbal told reporters in Mirpur.

Tamim praised Mehidy’s tenure, which included victories in four of his last five series in charge, but said his dip in batting form prompted the move.

“Mehidy as a cricketer for Bangladesh is more important than anything else…probably the level we’re accustomed to, we’re probably not seeing that right now, especially with his batting,” Tamim said. “I had a discussion with Mehidy, [and] he understands the point.”

Mehidy was handed the ODI captaincy on a 12-month basis in June last year, taking over from Najmul, who had briefly led the side across all formats.

Under Mehidy, Bangladesh won 10 of 20 ODIs, following a difficult start that saw them lose five of their first six matches and drop two consecutive series.

The team later rallied with four straight series wins at home against the West Indies, Pakistan, New Zealand and Australia, before losing an away series to Zimbabwe.

Litton has previous captaincy experience, having led Bangladesh in seven ODIs, including a 2022 series win over India.

Tamim also addressed the uncertain status of Bangladesh’s proposed series against India in September at home.

“I am very hopeful that they will come. Bangladesh is an extremely safe country,” he said.

Tamim said talks with the BCCI had been “very positive” so far and clarity was expected “very soon”.

Under the previous board, Bangladesh refused to play in India at this year’s T20 World Cup, citing security concerns after fast bowler Mustafizur Rahman was dumped by Indian Premier League team Kolkata Knight Riders.

“There are certain things that are beyond my control. They [government] also have to make a decision, I’m sure. Very soon, perhaps, we will find out whether the series is happening or not,” said Tamim.

Published in Dawn, July 30th, 2026

item.title: Hasina vows to return despite fearing for life. [ dawn ]
item.description:
NEW DELHI: Bangladesh’s fugitive ex-premier Sheikh Hasina said she was determined to return to her country by December despite fearing for her life.

“I may be killed. I may be arrested. I may be sent to prison,” Hasina, 78, said in an emailed response to questions by this news agency.

“I am fully aware of my fate. Still, I want to go back because my people are calling me.” Toppled in August 2024 by a student-led uprising that ended her 15-year, iron-fisted rule, Hasina fled by helicopter to India as crowds stormed her palace. The United Nations says up to 1,400 people were killed in crackdowns as she tried to cling to power.

In November, Hasina was found guilty by a Dhaka court of crimes against humanity and sentenced to be hanged — a verdict she described as “political vengeance dressed up as law”.

The former prime minister, who has been living in a secret location in India, insisted there was no pressure for her to return. Relations between India and Bangladesh, strained under the interim administration that took power after Hasina’s fall, have stabilised since Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman took office in February.

Dhaka has formally requested Hasina’s extradition — a request New Delhi has said is “under examination”. Hasina said the issue had “no connection” with her decision to return.

“I can say that I am staying in India with due respect and dignity,” she said. “Indian authorities have not discussed extradition with me. I myself have decided to return to my country.”

The Bangladeshi government has said it will ensure Hasina receives due legal process in all cases against her should she return. Rights groups have long accused Hasina’s former administration of abuses including the murder of rivals, suppression of opposition parties, rigged courts and one-sided elections.
